words.lemma: mitra- (voc., in the dual Mitra-Varuna phrase)
aṣ̌iia- (adj. nom.sg., 'belonging to aša', epithet of Sraoša)

cognate: Ved r̥tá- = Av aṣ̌a- (PIIr *Hr̥tá-, 'truth, cosmic order'); Ved drúh-/druhvan- = Av druj-/drəguuant- (PIIr *drugʰ-, 'deceit, the deceiver'); Ved r̥tā́van- = Av aṣ̌auuan- (exact suffixal equation, RV 1.122.9 vs Y31.17); secondarily Ved mitrá- = Av miϑra- with Ved abhi-drúh- 'deceiving (Mitra-Varuna)' ~ Av miϑrō aiβi.druxta- / miϑrō.druj- 'deceiving Mithra'
drift_or_renewal: Avestan has systematised the pair into the dualist aša/druj antithesis and personified druj as a demoness (daēuuī druxš); Vedic druh- stays a common noun for 'harm, deceit, fiend' and the r̥ta/druh opposition is occasional. The verb is renewed: Ved nud- 'thrust away', han- 'smite', dah- 'burn' vs Av vən- 'conquer', dā- zastaiiō 'hand over', pərəs- 'question' (VS18)
shared_syntax: In the anchors, a god with an epithet derived from r̥ta/aša (Ved r̥tāvŕ̥dh-, Av aṣ̌iia-) takes the druh-/druj- as its direct object in the accusative (druhvāṇaṃ … nudethe; drujim apərəsat̰), though the verbs are not related. The closer collocational match lies in the support passages, where r̥ta/aša is the means or ally by which the druh is overcome: Ved r̥téna … ápa drúhaḥ … āvar (RV 7.75.1), r̥téna drúhaḥ dahāmi (RV 1.133.1), druháḥ hantā́ … r̥tásya dhartári (RV 2.23.17) ~ Av aṣ̌ā drujim vəṇghaitī (Y48.1), aṣ̌āi … drujim/drujə̄m … zastaiiō (Y30.8, Y44.14).
context: Both anchors are ritual-religious texts that set a truth-god against the deceiver. AVP 4.38 invokes Mitra and Varuna, 'strengtheners of r̥ta, of true might', who drive off the druhvan and help the truthful man (satyāvan). VS18.36 is the dialogue in which Sraoša, 'the one belonging to aša', questions the druj about who makes her pregnant. The same two cognate abstracts are set against each other again and again: in the Gathas (Y30, 31, 32, 33, 43, 44, 46, 48, 49, 51) and in the Younger Avesta, where the Vīdēvdād refrains repeat it. A tight count gives about 50 distinct Avestan verses with both roots, about 20 of them in the Yasna. In the RV the two roots meet in 9 stanzas, several in the same sense (r̥ta holds or conquers the druh). Mitra is the guardian against druh in both traditions (RV 1.122.9, 8.47.1; Av miϑrō.druj-, VS4.5). A pair of two abstract nouns, each with exact cognates and kept in a fixed antithesis in the same theological role, is unlikely to come about by chance. Both are Indo-Iranian, so this is Proto-Indo-Iranian phraseology, not reconstructable further back as a phrase. The Avestan anchor is a late Vīdēvdād-type text, but the Gathic support shows the antithesis is old.
phrase: PIIr *Hr̥tá- vs *drugʰ- : 'the r̥ta-god repels / conquers the druh' (Ved r̥tāvŕ̥dh- … druhvāṇaṃ nud-; Av aṣ̌iia- … drujim; aṣ̌ā drujim vən-)

words.lemma: corp 'body', dat.pl. (ina c-corpaib 'in their bodies', i.e. eaten); slab leaves unlemmatized

cognate: Ir. cú/coin = Lat. canis/canes = Gk κύων/κύνες (*ḱwṓ); the bird term is renewed in each language (Ir. én, Lat. coruus/uulturius, Gk οἰωνός/γύψ)
drift_or_renewal: The bird word is renewed in each language. Latin breaks the pair into a list (raven, dogs, wolves), and the Irish adds wolves (cuanart) in its support passages. In the pivot the merism has become a boast that nothing will leave the besieged fort except what dogs carry in their bellies and birds in their claws.
shared_syntax: The dog and bird pair appears as the agents who consume the bodies of slain or cursed enemies: Ir. coin ina c-corpaib ocus eóin ina c-crobaib; Lat. … uoret … coruus / intestina canes; Gk ἑλώρια … κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε.
context: In all three the context is the same: a threat or curse that the enemy's body will be left unburied and eaten by dogs and carrion birds, as the mark of utter defeat. The Irish passage is Corc's message that only dogs, birds and armed men will come out of Conall's fort. Catullus 108 curses Cominius with his tongue to the vulture, his eyes to the raven, his guts to the dogs. Homer uses κύνες + οἰωνοί as a formula 12 times. The dog word is a strict cognate and holds its place in the pair, which argues for continuity. But the motif of the unburied dead given to dogs and birds is very general in the ancient world: it is common in Hebrew Bible curses, from which Christian Irish writers could take it directly, and in Akkadian texts. The Irish witness is Early Modern, from a ZCP OCR text. So the match may be typological or borrowed rather than inherited.
phrase: '(corpses as) prey for dogs and birds': Ir. coin … ocus eóin ~ Lat. coruus … canes ~ Gk κύνες … οἰωνοί

note: All 137 bundles read. Most pivots are Bandamanna saga, Íslendingabók or Menota law and Early Modern Irish OCR (Betha Colaim Chille, ZCP poems); partners are mostly late Greek prose (Galen, Plutarch, Strabo) with no shared context. Claim 1 (medium) comes from an Indo-Iranian partner pair in BC-9b9ad, where the ON pivot plays no part. Claim 2 (low) comes from the dogs-and-birds carrion merism, across BC-0539f (the Irish pivot) and BC-1a582 (the Catullus partner). Rejected: BC-5a171 ON eldr/maðr/dyrr vs RV 10.110.1 (generic); BC-5de94 Irish 'more angels than leaves or grass' (no cognate partner); BC-1a582 own pivot (an Irish lament without the beasts), so it is used only for its Catullus partner.
